summary.text: 能 is traditionally interpreted as a bear pictograph. The character is also attested for “be able” and “ability,” but the evidence here does not explain how those uses relate to the bear sense.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph is best explained as a depiction of a bear. The Han dictionary instead analyzes it as 肉 plus 㠯 as phonetic; paleographic discussion allows the 㠯-like shape to represent the bear’s transformed head, so a separate phonetic component is not established.

history.text: Some damaged Shang oracle-bone forms have been identified as 能 and interpreted as bear-like, but their use is unclear. A competing analysis rejects that identification and places securely identifiable examples in Western Zhou bronze inscriptions; the disagreement remains unresolved. Descriptions of the graphic sequence report the head changing toward 㠯, the body rendered as 月 (肉), and the feet arranged side by side.

The Han dictionary records 能 as a kind of bear and analyzes the graph as 肉 plus 㠯. Its explanation that the animal’s firmness and strength relate to 賢能 and 能傑 is that dictionary’s historical interpretation; it does not establish how the bear and ability uses developed.

uncertainties.text: The Shang identification and use remain disputed, and no dated first occurrence is established for the Western Zhou examples. The evidence does not show whether “be able” developed from the bear meaning or whether the graph came to write that word by another process; the bear’s spoken name is not independently known.

The Han dictionary’s analysis of 㠯 as phonetic is historically important, but paleographic discussion also allows it to reflect a transformed bear head. No independent phonetic role or component sound comparison is established.

senses.text: The Han dictionary defines 能 as a kind of bear, and historical pronunciation records list bear readings. The proposed Shang examples do not securely date this use because their identification and use are disputed.
A reported Western Zhou bronze use has 能 as a verb meaning “be able to.” This is the earliest ability use identified here; it does not establish the character’s original meaning.
Historical reports cite ability-related noun uses in Warring States-era texts. Modern definitions also include “ability,” but do not establish a further dated stage.

limitations.text: The bear and ability uses are separately attested, but their semantic relationship or a sound-based borrowing between them is not established. The evidence gives no independently known spoken name for the depicted bear to demonstrate a sound match.

overview.text: 能 is best understood as an old picture of a bear, though the identification of proposed Shang forms is disputed. It is also used for “be able” and “ability”; the evidence does not explain how those uses connect to the bear meaning.
